summary: Points out that benchmarking network devices has overlooked two factors that strongly affect results: the bit patterns in test packets, and how bit and byte stuffing change packet sizes on the wire. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: When testing how fast a network box is, the exact data inside test packets can change the answer. This warns testers to report and control those details.

questions: why test traffic content affects benchmark results
what is network benchmarking hash and stuffing
what is bit stuffing in ppp
what mac addresses should benchmark test traffic use
subtitle: Why the contents of test packets and link-layer stuffing quietly change network benchmark results, and what testers should do about it.

tldr.problem: Benchmarking methods require testers to declare load, packet length and similar factors, but not the addresses and other contents of test packets, and they ignore stuff bits and bytes that some link layers insert.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends pseudorandom, uniformly distributed addresses and ports in test traffic, and gives formulas for the probability of bit-stuffing and byte-stuffing so testers can reduce their offered load to match.
tldr.outcome: Following the guidelines makes results more repeatable and avoids accidentally congesting the device under test. It is Informational guidance for lab testing.

today: RFC 4814 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It adds guidance on top of earlier benchmarking methods such as RFC 2544 and RFC 2889.

sections.title: Two Overlooked Factors
sections.content:
Methodologies such as RFC 2544 and RFC 2889 require testers to declare parameters like traffic distribution and orientation, but not packet contents. Yet contents can matter as much. Some devices forward randomly addressed traffic without loss but drop many packets with nonrandom addresses, and two people following the same procedure can get very different results.

The second factor is stuffing: bits or bytes inserted by PPP with HDLC-like framing so test traffic is not confused with control characters. It adds variable overhead, and there was no standard way to work out how likely it is. The RFC covers both areas, and says benchmarking is limited to controlled laboratory testing on dedicated address space, with the test network not connected to production.
sections.eli5: Two small details in a speed test can change the answer a lot: what the test packets look like inside, and extra bits that some links add on their own.

sections.title: Why Packet Contents Matter
sections.content:
Many devices feed addresses into a hash to choose a forwarding path. The RFC gives an example from real devices: a switch with eight network processors (NP0 to NP7) that XORs the least significant 3 bits of the source and destination MAC addresses.

If the tester uses the pattern 00:00:PP:00:00:01, every address ends in 001, so the result is always 001 ^ 001 = 000. All traffic goes to NP0 and the switch can use only about 12.5 percent of its capacity. With 00:00:PP:00:00:RR, where RR is pseudorandom, the outcomes spread evenly and the device can use 100 percent.

Testers cannot always know a device's hash, and relying on that would break the black-box spirit of the Benchmarking Working Group. So the RFC instead recommends traffic patterns that avoid the effects of nonrandomness whatever the hash is.
sections.eli5: Imagine eight checkout lanes and a rule that picks the lane from the last digit of your ticket. If every test ticket ends in the same digit, seven lanes sit empty and you wrongly decide the shop is slow.

sections.title: Recommended Test Traffic Contents
sections.content:
Randomness here means a uniform distribution, and for any random bit pattern of length L the probability of that pattern SHOULD be 1 over 2 to the Lth power. The recommendations, layer by layer:

  • MAC addresses: use the pattern (RR & 0xFC):PP:PP:RR:RR:RR. The AND with 0xFC avoids multicast and locally administered addresses, PP:PP is the 1-indexed test instrument interface number, and the low 3 bytes are pseudorandom. Every address should be pseudorandom, not just the first of an incrementing series.
  • MPLS labels: uniformly random values from 16 to 1,048,575, avoiding the reserved labels 0 to 15 per RFC 3032.
  • IP addresses: a randomly distributed range, especially when testing equal cost multipath, since some implementations hash the source and destination addresses.
  • Ports: pseudorandom destination ports between 1 and 49151 and source ports between 1024 and 65535, unless specific ports are required.
  • Application layer: no specific pattern is recommended, but testers SHOULD know that contents can give nonrandom outcomes.

There is one exception. For some devices, such as IEEE 802.11 gear, different random addresses from trial to trial can hurt results. Testers MAY generate a pseudorandom or nonrandom set once, but the same MAC and IP addresses MUST be used in all trials.
sections.eli5: Use lots of different, shuffled addresses on the test packets so every lane gets used. If you shuffle, keep the same shuffle for every run so runs can be compared.

sections.title: Bit and Byte Stuffing
sections.content:
Stuffing is data dependent, so frames of equal length can take different amounts of space on the wire. If a tester aims for 95 percent of line rate and stuffing adds 1 percent, the real load is 96 percent, and a device with 95 percent capacity will drop traffic the tester never meant to cause.

Bit-stuffing (on bit-synchronous links such as T1/E1 and DS-3): per RFC 1662, a 0 bit is inserted after any five contiguous 1 bits, to avoid confusion with the flag 0x7E. The RFC models this as a state machine over random bits. For an infinitely long random string, the chance any bit causes a stuff is 1/62. That is about 1.6 percent, and the RFC recommends reducing the maximum intended load by 1.6 percent. For finite strings it gives f(L), the count of stuffs over all strings of length L, with expected stuffs f(L) / 2^L.

Byte-stuffing (PPP over SONET/SDH, RFC 2615): the flag 0x7E, the control escape 0x7D and any character set in the Async-Control-Character-Map (ACCM) are escaped. With default ACCM values, up to 34 characters are stuffed, so the chance for a random byte is 34 in 256, about 13.3 percent. With ACCM negotiated to 0x00 only 2 characters count, giving 2 in 256, about 0.8 percent. The RFC recommends negotiating an ACCM of 0x00 unless specific values are required, such as with L2TP, and reducing offered load by the matching percentage.

These percentages are approximations; for the greatest precision the actual load SHOULD be calculated from the test traffic. This applies to all measurements, including throughput.
sections.eli5: Some roads add a spacer after certain patterns to stop them being mistaken for a stop sign. The spacers take room, so a careful tester sends a little less to avoid overfilling the road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The pseudorandom patterns here need a uniform distribution but not strict unpredictability. The rand() function of many languages may be usable in a lab, though it is not sufficient for security applications. Test designers SHOULD understand the distribution created by their function and how seeding affects it.

The RFC also notes that RFC 2615 discusses a denial-of-service attack that sends characters needing stuffing and could consume up to 100 percent of bandwidth. Benchmarking networks generally SHOULD NOT be reachable by anyone other than the testers.
sections.eli5: Shuffling test packets is fine for a lab, but it is not secret-keeping. Keep the test network locked away from outsiders.
